content.rationale: Bottleneck Mahalanobis distance is sensitive to nearby held-out intents, while encoder-space distance captures broader domain shifts. Train-fitted robust scaling makes the two density signals comparable before additive fusion.

Features from in-scope queries should lie close to a principal subspace learned from training representations, whereas OOS queries tend to have larger residual components. Combining this train-calibrated residual with energy captures both representation-space and classifier uncertainty.

An OOS query may be globally similar to the training corpus while remaining atypical among examples of the class predicted by the classifier. Combining predicted-class and global cosine kNN distances measures both local intent support and broad in-domain coverage.
Within-class trailing covariance directions capture low-variance constraints of known intents. Queries that violate these constrained directions should receive larger OOS scores.

A query should be close to the representation distribution of the class predicted by the classifier, not merely close to some in-scope class. Per-class train-calibrated predicted-class Mahalanobis distances expose disagreement between classifier assignment and class-conditional feature support.

In-scope predictions tend to have both a clear top-two logit separation and a stronger centered logit magnitude. OOS queries often produce flatter, lower-contrast logit shapes, so train-calibrated deficits in both quantities are combined.

In-scope examples should have high cosine similarity to at least one class prototype in normalized bottleneck-feature space. OOS queries are expected to be poorly aligned with every learned intent direction.

Empirical CDF calibration puts logit energy and encoder-space Mahalanobis distance on the same train-derived scale. Their geometric fusion emphasizes queries that are simultaneously classifier-uncertain and atypical in representation space.

OOS inputs should distribute Dirichlet concentration more evenly across intent classes, whereas in-scope inputs typically exhibit a peaked concentration shape. Entropy of normalized Dirichlet concentrations measures this allocation pattern independently of total evidence.

Classifier energy is retained unchanged for confident items, while high-energy (uncertain) items receive an additional train-calibrated encoder-space atypicality penalty. This conditional use of Mahalanobis distance targets cases where logits alone are ambiguous.
Class-specific shrunk diagonal variances preserve low-variance intent constraints that a tied covariance washes out, while shrinkage keeps estimates stable for smaller classes.
The span of class means captures directions used to distinguish known intents. OOS queries can retain energy in the orthogonal remainder that is not explained by this discriminative subspace.

A ViM-style virtual OOS logit is formed from the norm outside a train-fitted principal feature subspace. In-scope examples should be explained by that subspace, while residual-heavy examples receive higher virtual-class posterior mass.
Local Outlier Factor compares each query's neighborhood density with the densities of its nearest training neighbors, identifying queries that fall in sparse or locally inconsistent regions.

Low-variance within-class directions encode constraints that in-scope examples rarely violate. A predicted-class residual measured only in these trailing directions exposes samples that are incompatible with the assigned intent.

In-scope queries should be substantially closer to one class manifold than to competing class manifolds. OOS queries often have a small nearest-versus-second-nearest Mahalanobis gap, indicating ambiguous class-conditional support.

The top-two margin normalized by centered logit norm measures angular confidence rather than raw logit scale. OOS queries should have a smaller fraction of their logit energy concentrated in the winning-class direction.

An in-scope query should align with the prototype of the class favored by the classifier. Probability-weighted prototype mismatch penalizes both weak directional support and disagreement between the classifier distribution and normalized feature geometry.

Train-calibrated percentile scores place classifier uncertainty and bottleneck-space atypicality on a common scale. Their probabilistic-OR fusion flags queries that are suspicious by either signal while emphasizing agreement between the two.

Energy is preserved for confident predictions, while only energy-uncertain queries receive an additional train-calibrated local feature-space outlier penalty. This targets uncertain queries that also lack nearby in-scope representation support.
A classifier-assigned intent should support the query under its own per-feature variance profile, with empirical-Bayes shrinkage stabilizing diagonal covariances for small classes.

Classifier-relevant feature directions are learned from train-only feature/logit cross-covariance. OOS queries should retain unusually large standardized feature energy outside this discriminative subspace.

A pooled representation that has large energy outside the train-fitted principal subspace is poorly explained by in-scope feature structure. Averaging its train-calibrated residual percentile with energy retains classifier uncertainty while emphasizing unexplained feature content.

Average distance to the nearest normalized encoder representations measures local in-scope support more smoothly than a single neighbor boundary. OOS queries should have consistently larger cosine-space distances to their closest known examples.

Trailing within-class covariance directions encode tight intent-specific constraints, while normalizing trailing residual energy by total partial-space residual reduces sensitivity to overall feature scale. OOS inputs should devote an unusually large fraction of their residual energy to these low-variance directions.

A known-intent query should be both close to its classifier-predicted class and more geometrically compatible with that class than with alternatives. Combining absolute predicted-class distance with a contrastive class-competition penalty exposes classifier and representation disagreement without reducing to nearest-class distance alone.

Tempered posterior entropy measures how broadly classifier evidence is distributed across intents after setting the temperature from train-time logit gaps. OOS queries should retain more competing intent mass and therefore have higher entropy than sharply concentrated in-scope predictions.

The classifier-selected intent should have a prototype direction aligned with an in-scope query. Low cosine similarity to the predicted class prototype identifies representation-classifier disagreement indicative of OOS inputs.

The normalized entropy of evidence above the Dirichlet prior measures how evenly class-specific evidence is distributed, rather than total evidence alone. OOS inputs should often lack a dominant intent-specific evidence pattern and therefore have higher evidence-shape entropy.
Energy remains the dominant score for confidently classified inputs, while a train-calibrated pooled-feature Mahalanobis distance is increasingly activated only when logits indicate uncertainty.

Class-specific shrunk diagonal variances model intent-dependent feature tolerances that a tied covariance cannot capture. A query is suspicious when its classifier-selected class assigns it an unusually large heteroscedastic residual relative to that class's training examples.

Class-mean directions span the representation subspace most directly associated with intent discrimination. OOS queries should have unusually large train-calibrated residual energy outside this supervised subspace.

Bottleneck and encoder-space densities capture complementary near-OOS and far-OOS deviations. Train-calibrated density percentiles make their tails comparable before an additive reliability-weighted fusion.

A ViM-style virtual OOS logit is formed from representation energy outside a train-fitted principal subspace and compared directly against the classifier's in-scope logit evidence. Inputs with large unexplained residual representations receive high virtual-class probability even when one known-class logit is moderately large.

The distance to a moderately distant neighbor in raw bottleneck space estimates local in-scope support while being less sensitive than the single nearest example to duplicates or accidental close matches. OOS queries should lie in lower-density regions and therefore have larger k-neighbor distances.

Low-variance within-class directions encode tight constraints that in-scope representations should satisfy. A large fraction of residual energy concentrated in these trailing directions indicates poor compatibility with known intent manifolds.

A query should be compatible with the class selected by the classifier, not merely with some nearby known class. Class-conditional empirical tail calibration makes unusually large predicted-class Mahalanobis distances comparable across intents.

Each in-scope intent has a characteristic centered logit profile, including how strongly non-winning intents are suppressed. OOS queries that are assigned to a known intent but exhibit an atypical class-conditional logit shape receive a larger standardized residual score.

Energy and pooled-space Mahalanobis distance capture classifier uncertainty and representation atypicality on different raw scales. Train-fitted empirical percentiles put both signals on a common tail-probability scale before averaging them.

EDL out-of-scope inputs should often lack the class-specific evidence dominance seen for in-scope examples. A train-calibrated top-versus-runner-up evidence margin detects atypical Dirichlet concentration shape rather than total evidence or vacuity.
Energy remains the score for confident inputs, while feature distance contributes only when energy is uncertain and is unusually large relative to the train-time energy--distance relation.

A query should be close under the intent-specific feature tolerances of the two intents favored by its classifier logits. A shrunk diagonal covariance captures heterogeneous per-intent variation while top-two posterior mixing penalizes representation-logit disagreement.

Bottleneck and encoder densities are calibrated separately within the classifier-predicted intent, so near-OOS and domain-shift deviations are comparable without relying on a global density scale. Train-fitted reliability weights are constrained to retain both views, preventing either representation space from collapsing the fusion into a duplicate single-density ranking.
A global train-fitted principal subspace captures dominant in-scope encoder variation, while OOS inputs should retain more energy in discarded residual directions.
A local neighborhood with both large average distance and mixed intent labels indicates weak in-scope support: OOS queries should be farther from training examples and less class-pure locally.

Low-variance within-class directions encode constraints that normal intent examples satisfy tightly. A large classifier-selected-class residual in these trailing directions indicates incompatibility with known intent manifolds.

An in-scope representation should both fit the classifier-predicted intent and be distinctly closer to that intent than to competing intent means. OOS queries tend to have a large predicted-class residual, a weak representation-space class margin, or both.

In-scope examples typically exhibit a class-specific dominant top logit relative to the overall logit spread. OOS queries often have a weaker normalized top-two separation even when their raw maximum probability or energy appears confident.

A query should be angularly compatible with the prototype of the class predicted by the classifier, and that compatibility should be unusually strong relative to competing intent prototypes. Class-conditional train calibration makes low predicted-prototype cosine and weak angular separation high OOS scores.

Classifier-predicted-intent calibration makes logit uncertainty and predicted-class representation mismatch comparable on train-fitted percentile scales. OOS inputs should simultaneously have unusually weak logit evidence or atypical encoder-space distance.

The normalized Dirichlet concentration profile encodes how evidence is distributed across intents independently of total evidence. OOS inputs should exhibit an atypical profile for their predicted intent even when vacuity or energy is not unusual.

Energy retains control for train-calibrated confident predictions, preserving its useful ranking there, while a pooled-space Mahalanobis score progressively replaces it for uncertain predictions where representation support is more informative.

Per-intent diagonal variances expose representation coordinates that violate the predicted intent's individual tolerance profile. Counting and sizing coordinatewise tail exceedances detects distributed mismatch that a single pooled Mahalanobis score can dilute.

Class-mean directions capture variation that separates known intents, while the orthogonal remainder captures within-intent constraints that OOS queries need not satisfy. Calibrating residual energy by predicted intent accounts for classes with different residual variability.

A ViM-style residual norm measures feature energy outside the dominant in-scope bottleneck subspace, while energy captures classifier uncertainty. Train-calibrated tail scales combine these complementary signals.

An in-scope query should be supported by nearby examples from the intent predicted by its logits, not merely by nearby examples from other intents. The ratio of predicted-intent neighborhood distance to global neighborhood distance detects local representation-logit disagreement.

Low-variance within-intent directions encode constraints that ordinary in-scope examples satisfy. This uses classifier-predicted-class prototypes and train-calibrated trailing-subspace residuals, so unusually large residual energy is scored as OOS.

Known-intent examples are typically distinctly closer to one class prototype than to the next-best prototype. OOS inputs often remain far from every class and have a weak nearest-versus-second-nearest distance separation.

After removing the arbitrary common logit offset, in-scope examples tend to have larger class-conditional logit-vector norms than OOS examples. Predicted-intent calibration prevents naturally low-confidence known intents from dominating the score.

Energy and classifier-selected Mahalanobis mismatch capture complementary logit and representation failures. Per-predicted-intent empirical calibration puts both signals on a common train-derived tail-probability scale before combining them.

EDL concentration shapes encode which non-predicted intents receive residual evidence. An OOS query should exhibit an uncommon predicted-intent/runner-up confusion pattern or an atypical runner-up evidence magnitude.

Energy is retained for confidently supported predictions, while a train-calibrated feature-space mismatch is activated only in the uncertain energy tail. This targets queries whose logits are ambiguous and whose pooled representation is also atypical for every known intent.

A shrunk diagonal covariance gives each intent its own coordinatewise tolerance while borrowing strength from global feature variability. Queries with unusually low likelihood under their logit-predicted intent receive high train-calibrated OOS scores.

Class-mean directions primarily encode intent-discriminative variation, so removing them isolates within-intent residual structure. OOS queries may project plausibly onto known intent directions but lack local support in the residual manifold occupied by in-scope examples.

In-scope bottleneck features concentrate near a dominant training-feature subspace, whereas OOS inputs often retain larger components in its orthogonal residual space. A train-calibrated residual norm provides a ViM-style OOS signal without relying on evaluation-set statistics.

In-scope queries should remain supported across both very local and broader neighborhoods, while OOS queries often become increasingly isolated as neighborhood scale grows. Combining train-calibrated kNN distances at multiple scales reduces sensitivity to accidental single-neighbor matches.

Low-variance within-class eigen-directions encode tight representation constraints that known intents satisfy. The maximum whitened deviation in these trailing directions detects a localized constraint violation that residual-energy sums can dilute.

An in-scope query's logit-predicted intent should also be its closest class prototype in whitened representation space. A large predicted-class distance relative to the best competing prototype signals classifier-representation disagreement characteristic of OOS inputs.

After removing the arbitrary common logit offset, in-scope examples tend to have class-conditional centered-logit magnitudes typical of their predicted intent. A train-calibrated lower-tail score flags flattened or unusually weak logit shapes beyond MSP and energy.

Angular alignment to the prototype of the classifier-selected intent should be typical for in-scope queries. Class-conditional train calibration flags unusually weak cosine agreement without letting naturally diffuse intents dominate.

Logit uncertainty and feature-space atypicality provide complementary OOS evidence. Train-derived empirical tail calibration maps energy and Mahalanobis distance to a shared scale before combining them.
